title: The Problem With Split Buttons
intro: A split button pairs a labelled primary action with a small dropdown arrow. Users treat it as one button, read the chevron as decoration, and never find what's behind it.

learn.title: What users actually do
learn.text:
In Calabro's recent tests, **about 80% of participants clicked only the labelled side**, never realising there was more under the arrow.

Users who *intended* to open the menu often triggered the primary action instead — an accidental purchase, or the wrong state.

The tiny chevron reads as decoration.

try.q: Roughly what share of participants clicked only the labelled side in his tests?
options: About 80%
About 20%
About half
Nearly everyone, apart from screen reader users
try.explain: They never realised there was more functionality under the arrow.

left.label: What the team assumes
items: Two clear actions in one control

learn.title: Why stakeholders keep asking for them
learn.text:
Split buttons let a team avoid a hard decision about priority. “We can put every possible action in one button? Cool.”

It feels like a compromise that saves space. **Saving space is not the same as reducing cognitive load.**

Three e-commerce clients asked Calabro to validate theirs. All three pushed back — and during a demo, one of them mis-clicked the arrow himself.

try.q: What hard question does a split button let a team avoid?
options: Which action is primary
Which users are the target
Which platform to design for first
Whether the feature should exist at all
try.explain: That is exactly the question the pattern is designed to dodge.

learn.title: What to do instead
learn.text:
If the secondary actions matter, expose them as **separate buttons** or a clear **overflow menu** — not hidden behind an ambiguous chevron attached to a primary action.

Aesthetic adjustments don't help: one client tried multiple rounds of visual refinement to emphasise the split, and end-user behaviour didn't change at all.

try.q: A client emphasises the visual split between the two halves. What happens to behaviour?
options: Nothing changes
Discovery roughly doubles
Mis-clicks fall but discovery stays low
Screen reader users benefit, others don't
try.explain: Multiple rounds of visual refinement didn't alter end-user behaviour.

options: A labelled action plus a small dropdown arrow
Two buttons separated by a divider line
A button that changes label based on context
A toggle that reveals a second action on hover
test.explain: The two halves do different things.

test.q: What does the chevron communicate to most users?
options: Nothing — it reads as decoration
That the button has a secondary menu
That the action is irreversible
That more options load after clicking
test.explain: Which is why hidden options stay hidden.

test.q: Why is a split button especially risky in a destructive flow?
options: Users trigger the primary action by mistake
Destructive actions need confirmation dialogs
The arrow is too small for touch targets
Screen readers announce the label twice
test.explain: Intending the menu and hitting the action is a common failure in testing.

test.q: What does Calabro recommend in place of a split button?
options: Separate buttons or a clear overflow menu
A dropdown containing every action
A context menu on right-click
A single button plus a help tooltip
test.explain: Force the priority decision instead of hiding it.

test.q: Why doesn't “our users are on the site all the time” hold up?
options: Even that client mis-clicked during the demo
Frequent users read chevrons more carefully
Repeat visitors avoid dropdown menus
Site frequency doesn't affect motor accuracy
test.explain: Familiarity didn't rescue the pattern, even for its defender.
